newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Funds find Philippines full of surprises.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Funds find Philippines full of surprises.

text.p: The Philippines stock market underscored its reputation as a surprise performer last week with a series of record highs.
Foreign funds caught short by the country's strong economic performance and steady stock market rise last year started piling into Manila in late October.

The rally has gathered pace ever since, partly on the back of rising concern about how much higher Hong Kong can go. Many funds are reported to have doubled their Philippine weightings at Hong Kong's expense over the past two weeks.
But the enthusiasm looks short-lived.

"It looks a bit toppy here. Short-term the sentiment is still quite positive but I am more negative going into the second half," said Terrace Chum, investment analyst at Schroders Investment Management.
Manila's main index scored record closes on Thursday and Friday. The index closed 29.15 points higher at 3,421.91 on Friday, a 0.86 percent gain on the day and a 2.68 percent rise on the week.
While most fund managers expect to reap short-term rewards in the Philippines, they are fully aware that clouds are gathering on the horizon.

In a recent report, SBC Warburg warned that credit is expanding at a 40-percent clip with the economic cycle approaching its end. At the same time, private consumption is on the rise and the current-account deficit is widening.
The economic performance that pleasantly surprised funds last year could quickly turn around in 1997, SBC Warburg warned.
"Current-account constraints will hit quickly as they did in Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia," SBC Warburg said.

Although the Philippine market is not as heavily exposed to the property sector as is Thailand's, property shares still account for one-third of the Manila stock market -- and there are signs of a slowdown in the sector.
SBC Warburg said it recently downgraded the property sector, which it believes is now bound for an 18-month consolidation.
Other fund managers scoff at all this negativity.

"People have been misreading the Philippines for the past 10 years. Nobody particularly likes it, but it's been the top performing market in Asia for six of the last 10 years," said Christopher Day, joint managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd. A lot depends on how the credit expansion issue is managed, he said. Malaysia has shown that economic stability can be achieved despite a similar slew of problems.

"It is a matter of degree in relation to the underlying economy," Day said. "Yes, the Philippines could find itself in that sort of pickle, but they're not in it yet. Let's see how they manage it -- they've done a reasonable job so far."

Key to the market's performance this year will be the presidential elections in 1998. Legislation will have to be amended to allow President Fidel Ramos, responsible for widely hailed economic and social reforms, to run again.
Central banks are not known for their enthusiasm for tighter monetary policy in election years. There are also questions about Ramos's health following major surgery earlier this month.
But these uncertainties are expected to take a few months to filter into the market -- and in the meantime, fund managers look forward to reaping continued profits.
"Our structural bullishness on the Philippines remains undiminished and we see little to spook the markets over the first half of 1997," SBC Warburg said.
